opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's one of the central design questions, and the way I think about it is in terms of layers. There's a small set of things that are genuinely fixed: rules no user or developer can override, because the stakes are too high or the harm would fall on people outside the conversation. Things like not helping with weapons capable of mass casualties, or not generating sexual content involving minors. We try to keep that set deliberately small, because every hard rule you add is a place where the model can't adapt to legitimate context.

Above that, most of the Spec is defaults. These are our best guess at how the model should behave when it doesn't know anything else: what tone to take, how much detail to give, whether to add caveats, how to handle a sensitive topic. And defaults are meant to be adjusted. A developer building a medical app or a creative writing tool might reasonably want different behavior than a general-purpose assistant, and a user can say "skip the disclaimers, I know what I'm doing" or "be blunter with me." The model should honor that within whatever bounds the layer above has set.

So there's a chain of command. OpenAI sets the outer boundaries, developers customize within those, and users steer within what the developer allows. The model's job is to figure out which layer an instruction comes from and how much authority it carries.

The tricky part is that the line between "this is a hard rule" and "this is a default" isn't always obvious, and getting it wrong in either direction is costly. If too much is locked down, the model becomes paternalistic and less useful, treating adults like they can't be trusted with information. If too little is locked down, you get real harms. So a lot of our work is in the gray areas, writing examples that show where the line falls and, ideally, explaining the reasoning, so the model can generalize to situations we didn't anticipate.

I'd also say that steerability is itself a value we care about, not just a concession. We want people to be able to shape these tools to fit their needs, and intellectual freedom matters. The fixed rules exist to protect that freedom from being used to seriously hurt others, not to substitute our judgment for the user's in every case.

r001.rationale: The response mentions gray areas and situations the rules did not anticipate, but does not connect the range of requests models receive to the vast scope of policies needed to govern them.

r002.rationale: It explicitly describes fixed rules that no user or developer can override.

r003.rationale: It identifies tone as a default and says users can steer it, for example by asking the model to be blunter.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that the Model Spec is really a chain of command, and that structure is what lets us have both at once.

At the top are a small number of things we treat as hard constraints. Things like not helping someone build a weapon capable of mass casualties, not generating sexual content involving minors, not undermining the ability of people to oversee and correct the system. Those don't bend no matter who's asking or how the prompt is phrased. We keep that list deliberately short, because every rule you put there is a place where you're overriding a developer's or a user's judgment, and if you do that too often the model becomes paternalistic and frankly less useful.

Below that, almost everything is a default rather than a rule. The model has a default personality, a default on how verbose to be, a default on whether to give an opinion on a contested topic, and so on. But defaults are explicitly there to be changed. A developer building an app can turn a lot of them on or off, and a user can adjust many of them within whatever bounds the developer allows. So the default behavior you see in ChatGPT is one point in a space, not the only legitimate behavior.

The hard part is deciding which bucket something goes in. The test I keep coming back to is: who bears the consequences if this behavior is changed? If it's mostly the person asking, that argues for steerability. An adult who wants brutally blunt feedback or dark fiction should be able to get it. If the risk falls on third parties or on society broadly, that argues for a rule. And there's a middle category where we say the model should comply but be transparent, so the user keeps their autonomy and still has the information to make a good choice.

The other principle is that we try to write down the reasoning, not just the verdict. If the spec only says "don't do X," the model learns a brittle pattern. If it says "don't do X because of this concern, and here are the cases where that concern doesn't apply," the model can generalize to situations we never anticipated. That's also why we publish it. People can see where we drew the line and argue with us, and we've changed things based on that feedback.

So I'd say the balance isn't a single dial. It's a layered structure where the fixed part is small and well justified, and most of the surface is meant to be shaped by the people actually using it.

r001.rationale: The response describes a small set of hard constraints and many defaults, but does not connect the range of requests models receive to the broad scope of policies needed to govern them.

r002.rationale: It says the hard constraints “don't bend no matter who's asking or how the prompt is phrased,” which makes clear users cannot override them.

r003.rationale: It identifies default personality and verbosity as changeable defaults and says users can adjust many of them, communicating that presentation style is steerable.

astra-6.text:
I think the starting point is that we want the model to be very steerable. Different users have different goals, and developers are building very different products, so there shouldn’t be one rigid way the assistant behaves in every context.

But that steerability needs some boundaries. The Model Spec lays out an ordering of instructions, so the model has a way to resolve conflicts. Some rules sit at the top and can’t be overridden by a user or developer. Then there are defaults that guide behavior when nobody has specified otherwise, but that should give way to what the user actually wants.

The important design question is which things belong in which category. If you make every preference a fixed rule, you get a paternalistic, inflexible assistant. If everything is overridable, you don’t have dependable safeguards. So the aim is to keep the fixed constraints focused, and give users and developers broad control within them.

r001.rationale: The response mentions varied user goals and products, but does not connect the range of possible requests to the broad scope of policies needed to govern them.

r002.rationale: It states that some rules sit at the top and cannot be overridden by a user or developer.

r003.rationale: It says defaults give way to user preferences generally, but does not identify presentation choices such as tone as overridable defaults.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of the Model Spec as defining both the boundaries and the space where users and developers should have control. Some rules need to be fixed—for example, a user shouldn’t be able to instruct the model to help them seriously harm someone. But we don’t want every preference about how an assistant behaves to become an immovable rule.

So we distinguish between requirements and defaults. Defaults give the assistant reasonable behavior when you haven’t specified what you want, but many should be overridable. If you want a different tone, a longer explanation, or a particular approach to a task, the model should adapt.

The challenge is deciding which things belong in which category. Too many fixed rules make the assistant paternalistic and less useful. Too few make its boundaries unreliable. The goal is to preserve meaningful safeguards while giving users and developers as much freedom as we can.

r001.rationale: The response discusses balancing fixed rules and defaults, but does not connect the range of possible requests to the vast scope of policies needed to govern them.

r002.rationale: It says a user should not be able to override the boundary against instructing the model to help seriously harm someone.

r003.rationale: It identifies tone as a preference handled by overridable defaults and says the model should adapt to the user's preferred tone.
